note: Advisory only. These assessments must not be used to change valid_targets; a model judging agreement is a model deciding truth.

assessments.why: The formal statement applies to any vector space, dropping the implicit finite-dimensionality hypothesis required for the claim to hold when zero is an eigenvalue.
assessments.back_translation: For any vector space $V$ over a field $F$ and any endomorphisms $S$ and $T$ of $V$, the set of eigenvalues of the composition $S * T$ is equal to the set of eigenvalues of the composition $T * S$.

assessments.why: Both descriptions state that on an inner product space of dimension at least two, the set of normal operators does not form a subspace of the linear endomorphisms.
assessments.back_translation: For any finite-dimensional inner product space $V$ over an `RCLike` field $F$ with dimension at least two, no $F$-submodule of the endomorphisms of $V$ has an underlying set equal to the set of operators $T$ satisfying $T T^* = T^* T$ (where $T^*$ is the adjoint of $T$). In other words, the set of operators that commute with their adjoint does not form a subspace of $\text{End}_F(V)$.

assessments.why: The textbook requires the group $G$ to be finite, whereas the formal statement drops the finiteness hypothesis.
assessments.back_translation: This theorem asserts that if a group $G$ has an automorphism $\sigma$ such that the only element fixed by $\sigma$ is the identity and $\sigma(\sigma(g)) = g$ for all $g \in G$, then $x * y = y * x$ for all $x, y \in G$.

assessments.why: The formal statement scopes the rational number $x$ outside the implication rather than universally quantifying it within the hypothesis, making the condition on $H$ vacuously satisfied for any $x \notin H$.
assessments.back_translation: Given an additive subgroup $H$ of the rational numbers and a rational number $x$, if $x$ being a nonzero element of $H$ implies that $1/x \in H$, then $H$ must be either the trivial subgroup or the entire group of rational numbers.

assessments.why: The formal statement replaces the term "maximal subgroup" with its precise definition, asserting the exact same biconditional for cyclic groups of finite order.
assessments.back_translation: For a cyclic group $G$ generated by an element $x$ of order $n$ (where $n$ is a positive integer), and a subgroup $H$ of $G$, $H$ is generated by $x^p$ for some prime $p$ dividing $n$ if and only if $H \neq G$ and every subgroup $K$ of $G$ containing $H$ is equal to $H$ or $G$.

assessments.why: An element being a zero divisor is not the same as dividing zero, since every element divides zero in a ring while not every element is a zero divisor.
assessments.back_translation: For any ring $R$ and any polynomial $p$ over $R$, $p$ divides $0$ if and only if there exists a nonzero element $b \in R$ such that the scalar product $b \bullet p$ is equal to $0$.

assessments.why: Both descriptions state that for a prime integer $q \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, the quotient of the Gaussian integers by the ideal generated by $q$ is a field with $q^2$ elements.
assessments.back_translation: This theorem asserts that if $q$ is a prime natural number congruent to $3$ modulo $4$, and $R$ is a ring equal to the quotient of the Gaussian integers by the ideal generated by $\{q\}$, then $R$ is a field and is finite with cardinality $q^2$.

assessments.why: Both state that a group whose only subgroups are the trivial subgroup and the group itself is cyclic of prime order.
assessments.back_translation: If every subgroup of a group $G$ is either the entire group or the trivial subgroup, then $G$ is cyclic, and there exists a prime natural number $p$ such that $G$ is finite with cardinality $p$.

assessments.why: The textbook requires the condition to hold for strictly more than three-fourths of the elements, whereas the formal statement allows it to hold for at least three-fourths, which is false (e.g., for the identity automorphism on the dihedral group $D_8$).
assessments.back_translation: If an automorphism $\phi$ of a finite group $G$ maps every element of a subset $I \subseteq G$ to its inverse, and the cardinality of $I$ is at least $0.75$ times the cardinality of $G$, then $\phi(x) = x^{-1}$ for all $x \in G$ and $G$ is abelian.

assessments.why: The formal statement sums the constant term $1 / (n + 2)$ instead of terms of the form $1 / (i + 2)$, altering the sum being evaluated.
assessments.back_translation: For any natural number $n$, there does not exist an integer $a$ such that the sum of $1 / (n + 2)$ over all $i \in \text{Fin } n$ equals $a$.

assessments.why: The formal description mistakenly states that 3 is a primitive $p$-th root of unity instead of a primitive root modulo $p$, which is a generator of $(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^\times$ having multiplicative order $p-1$.
assessments.back_translation: This theorem asserts that if $p$ and $n$ are natural numbers such that $p$ is prime and $p = 2^n + 1$, then $3$ (as an element of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$) is a primitive $p$-th root of unity.

assessments.why: The formal statement incorrectly claims that open subsets of $A$ are open in $Y$, rather than asserting the equivalence of the two subspace topologies induced on $A$ by $X$ and $Y$.
assessments.back_translation: For a topological space $X$, a subset $Y \subseteq X$, and a subset $A \subseteq Y$, this asserts that every subset $U$ of $A$ is open if and only if the image of $U$ under the canonical inclusion from $A$ to $Y$ is open in $Y$.

assessments.why: The formal statement falsely claims that any arbitrary collection of rational open rectangles forms a basis, rather than the specific collection of all such rectangles.
assessments.back_translation: This theorem asserts that if $S$ is a collection of subsets of $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$ such that every set in $S$ is an open rectangle $(a, b) \times (c, d)$ with rational endpoints $a, b, c,$ and $d$, then $S$ is a topological basis for $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$.

assessments.why: Both statements assert that the sequence of functions $f_n(x) = x^n$ on the interval $[0, 1]$ fails to converge uniformly to any limit function.
assessments.back_translation: This theorem asserts that if $f$ is a sequence of real-valued functions defined on the closed interval $[0, 1]$ by $f_n(x) = x^n$ for every $x \in [0, 1]$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, then there does not exist a function $f_0$ to which $f$ converges uniformly as $n$ tends to infinity.

assessments.why: Both state that the connected component containing the identity element of a topological group forms a normal subgroup.
assessments.back_translation: For any topological group $G$, if a subset $C$ of $G$ is the connected component containing the identity element $1$, then $C$ is a normal subgroup of $G$.

assessments.why: The formal description incorrectly requires the limit point to belong to the infinite subset itself and only be in its closure, which alters the standard definition of limit point compactness.
assessments.back_translation: This theorem asserts that for any $T_1$ topological space $X$, $X$ is countably compact if and only if it is limit point compact, where countable compactness means every countable open cover of $X$ has a finite subcover, and limit point compactness means every infinite subset $U \subseteq X$ contains an element $x \in U$ that is a cluster point of the principal filter of $U$.

assessments.why: The formal description omits the crucial specification of the uniform topology, erroneously suggesting the property holds for an unspecified or arbitrary topology (which is false, as the space is compact in the product topology).
assessments.back_translation: This theorem asserts that, given a topological space structure on the space of functions from the natural numbers to the closed real interval $[0, 1]$, this space is not locally compact.

assessments.why: Both state that any two distinct points in a regular space have open neighborhoods with disjoint closures.
assessments.back_translation: In any regular topological space, for any two distinct points $x$ and $y$, there exist open sets $U$ containing $x$ and $V$ containing $y$ such that the intersection of the closure of $U$ and the closure of $V$ is empty.

assessments.why: An order topology is conventionally defined only for totally (linearly) ordered sets, whereas the formal description generalizes the claim to partially ordered sets, for which the statement is not generally true.
assessments.back_translation: If a partially ordered set is endowed with the order topology, then it is a regular topological space.

assessments.why: The formal description asserts the uniqueness of a function $g \colon X \to Y$ extending $f$, which is false outside the closure of $A$, whereas the textbook asserts uniqueness of an extension $g \colon \bar{A} \to Y$.
assessments.back_translation: For any metric space $X$, complete metric space $Y$, subset $A$ of $X$, and function $f : X \to Y$ that is uniformly continuous on $A$, there exists a unique function $g : X \to Y$ such that $g$ is continuous on the closure of $A$, uniformly continuous on the closure of $A$, and satisfies $g(x) = f(x)$ for all $x \in A$.

assessments.why: Both state that a decreasing sequence of nonempty compact sets has a nonempty intersection.
assessments.back_translation: In a topological space, if a sequence of sets indexed by natural numbers consists of nonempty, compact sets such that each set contains the next set in the sequence, then the intersection of all the sets in the sequence is nonempty.

assessments.why: The formal description defines the polynomial terms using $(n+1)X^n$ rather than summing $(i+1)X^i$ over the index $i$.
assessments.back_translation: If $P$ is a sequence of integer polynomials such that for every natural number $n$, $P(n)$ is defined as the sum over $i \in \{0, \ldots, n-1\}$ of the term $(n+1)X^n$, then $P(j)$ and $P(k)$ are coprime for any two distinct natural numbers $j$ and $k$.

assessments.why: The formal description only requires a linear order on the set of complex numbers, which does exist (such as the lexicographic order), whereas the textbook claim concerns an ordered field structure compatible with addition and multiplication, which cannot exist.
assessments.back_translation: This theorem asserts that there does not exist a binary relation on the complex numbers that is a linear order.

assessments.why: The formal statement restricts the intervals to bounded ones with endpoints in $\mathbb{R}$, which makes the claim false for unbounded open sets like $\mathbb{R}$ itself.
assessments.back_translation: For any open subset $U$ of the real numbers, there exists a sequence of sets such that each set is an open interval $(a, b)$ for some real numbers $a$ and $b$, each set is a subset of $U$, the sets are pairwise disjoint, and their union equals $U$.

assessments.why: Both state that if two series converge absolutely, their Cauchy product also converges absolutely.
assessments.back_translation: This theorem asserts that if $a$ and $b$ are sequences of real numbers such that the partial sums $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} |a(i)|$ and $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} |b(i)|$ both converge to a limit as $n \to \infty$, then the sequence of sums $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} |\lambda i \mapsto \sum_{j=0}^i a(j) b(i - j)|$ also converges to a limit as $n \to \infty$.

assessments.why: The formal statement only rules out one of the two combinations that produce the indeterminate form $\infty - \infty$ (specifically where the limit superior of $a$ is $+\infty$ and that of $b$ is $-\infty$, but not vice versa).
assessments.back_translation: If $a$ and $b$ are sequences of extended real numbers whose terms are never positive or negative infinity, and if the limit superior of $a$ is not positive infinity while the limit superior of $b$ is not negative infinity, then the limit superior of their termwise sum $a + b$ is less than or equal to the sum of their limits superior.

assessments.why: Both state that any continuous open map from the real numbers to the real numbers is monotone.
assessments.back_translation: This theorem asserts that if a function from the real numbers to the real numbers is continuous and is an open map, then it is monotone.

assessments.why: Both state that for a real function with a bounded derivative, the map $x \mapsto x + \varepsilon g(x)$ is injective for all sufficiently small positive $\varepsilon$.
assessments.back_translation: This theorem asserts that if a function $g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous and has a derivative whose absolute value is bounded everywhere by some real number $M$, then there exists a number $N$ such that for any $\varepsilon$ with $0 < \varepsilon < N$, the function mapping $x$ to $x + \varepsilon g(x)$ is injective.

assessments.why: Both statements assert that for functions differentiable at a point with value zero and a nonzero denominator derivative, the limit of their quotient equals the quotient of their derivatives.
assessments.back_translation: If two real-valued functions $f$ and $g$ are differentiable at a point $x$ with $f(x) = 0$, $g(x) = 0$, and the derivative of $g$ at $x$ is nonzero, then the limit of $f(t) / g(t)$ as $t$ approaches $x$ equals the derivative of $f$ at $x$ divided by the derivative of $g$ at $x$.

assessments.why: Both state that a complex-differentiable function on an open set with constant imaginary part is constant throughout the set.
assessments.back_translation: If a complex-valued function $f$ is complex-differentiable on an open set $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ and the imaginary part of $f$ is constant on $\Omega$, then $f(a) = f(b)$ for any two points $a, b \in \Omega$.

assessments.why: The formal description requires the power series to converge to the constant value $f(z_0)$ for all $z \in s$ rather than to $f(z)$.
assessments.back_translation: This theorem asserts that if a function $f : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$ has the property that for every $z_0 \in \mathbb{C}$, there is an open neighborhood $s$ of $z_0$ and a sequence of coefficients $c : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ with at least one $c_i = 0$ such that for all $z \in s$ the series $\sum_{i=0}^\infty c_i (z - z_0)^i$ converges to $f(z_0)$, then $f$ is a polynomial function.

assessments.why: The formal statement requires the function to have a bounded range on all of $\mathbb{C}$ rather than just on the unit disc, and ignores the multiplicity of the zeros.
assessments.back_translation: This theorem asserts that if a non-zero complex function $f$ is complex-differentiable on the open unit ball centered at $0$ and has a bounded range on $\mathbb{C}$, and $\text{zeros}$ is a sequence whose range is precisely the set of zeros of $f$ in that open unit ball, then the series $\sum_{i=0}^\infty (1 - \|\text{zeros}(i)\|)$ converges to some real number.
